It is the lane beyond the stream, where the lights blink in the windows. The road is wide, the grass is short, and the gravel crunches underfoot. I avoid it at night. The lights are too bright, and the cars are too loud. I prefer the wood, the stream, and the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is a mix of fields and the road. The fields are dry and hard in the summer, but in the spring they are green and full of voles. The road is busy with cars and lights, and it's dangerous for small animals. I stay away from it at night. I prefer the meadow and the stream. The meadow is soft and full of insects, and the stream is cool and has fish. I can hear the water from a distance.

Open land near my home is the meadow beyond the lane. It is dry in summer, muddy in spring, and full of voles. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The field is bounded by the lane on one side and the stream on the other. I can see the lights of the village from there, but I avoid them. The meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a field of grass and stones, with a stream running through it. The road is loud and bright, and the lights from the houses shine like fireflies. I avoid it, but I hear the cars and the people. The field is good for voles, but the road is bad. I call from the hedgerow, and the voles come. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and flat, with patches of bare earth and scattered stones. The wind moves through it, and sometimes I hear the low hum of a distant car. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can see the lights of the houses from the trees. It is a field of meadow and a road. The meadow is green in spring, brown in fall. The road is noisy with cars and lights. I avoid it. The meadow is where I hunt. Mice, voles, sometimes a shrew. I call from the oak, and they come. The road is not for me. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is a mix of meadows and a gravel road. The meadows are soft and full of voles in the spring, but they dry out in summer. The road is noisy with cars and people, and it's dangerous for small creatures. I avoid it unless I'm hunting at night. The hedgerows on either side are good for cover. I can hear the traffic from my perch.

Open land? The meadow near my home is dry and cracked in summer, but in spring it's green with dandelions and clover. The lane is wide and lit up at night, so I can see the cars and the lights. It's noisy with traffic and dogs, but I don't care. I keep to the wood and the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a lane of clay and stone with a ditch on one side and a fence on the other. The ditch is a good place to hunt. I can hear the traffic from the road, and the lights from the houses. The fence is old and broken, and I can see through the gaps. The lane is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind and the water. I do not like the lights, they blind me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the road. It runs east of the hollow and is wide and dark. I can see it from the edge of the woods, where the lane ends. It moves with cars and lights, and the noise is loud. I avoid it, but I hear the cars at night. They are not like us.

Open land near my home is the road and the field beyond. The road is lit up at night, and the field is full of voles. I hear them running under the grass. The field is not safe, but I know where to hunt. I sit on the fence post and wait. The voles come out at dusk. I can see them from the top of the post. I swoop down and catch them. The field is my hunting ground. It is not like the wood

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is soft and muddy after rain, and the grasses are tall. I can hear the voles scurrying beneath the surface. In the dusk, the lights of the village flicker like fireflies. I avoid the road, where the cars rumble and the dogs bark. I prefer the quiet of the meadow, where I can hunt without fear.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the fieldmice come out at dusk. I hear them scurry, and I wait. It is soft underfoot, and the scent of damp earth rises from the soil. I do not like it much. Too much noise, too many scents. I prefer the wood.

The open land near my home is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and soft underfoot, with patches of bare earth and a few clumps of heather. The wind moves through it, and sometimes it carries the scent of damp earth and the distant smell of woodsmoke from the village. I can hear the skylarks singing in the morning, and the foxes padding through the grass at dusk. It is a place of movement and sound, but I stay close to

The open land near my home is a mix of meadows and fields. It is mostly dry and hard underfoot, with some patches of soft earth where the rain has made it muddy. I can see the road from the hollow, and it runs through the meadows, lit by streetlights at night. The fields are where the voles and shrews run, and I often hear them scurrying beneath the soil. Open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with a path running through it. The grass is tall in spring, and the flowers bloom in summer. I can see the path from my perch, and I watch for voles and shrews that run along it. The meadow is quiet at night, but I hear the wind and the rustle of leaves. I sometimes fly over it to find food, but I prefer to stay close to the wood.

I fly low, just above the ground, over the meadow and the lane. I listen for the rustle of voles, the skitter of mice. The light fades, and the field turns to shadow. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. The mice come out. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find prey. The voles are out, and I follow their tracks in the grass. If I see a light, I fly higher. I know the lane well, the ditch, the old oak. I hunt where the light fades and the shadows grow.
I fly over the meadow, low and slow, past the stream. The light fades, and the voles stir. I listen for the rustle in the grass. If I hear it, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The mice come out. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and they freeze. Then I dive.

I fly up the oak first, then the ash, then the hawthorn, then the hawthorn again. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. The meadow is open, the field is open, the stream is open. I fly over the meadow, then the field, then the stream, then back to the oak. I hunt the voles and mice and the occasional shrew. I don't go far, but I

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light fades. The meadow is quiet then, and the voles come out. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. The light is gone, and the dark is here. I hunt by sound. I hear the rustle, the scratch, the squeak. I drop from the branch, silent as a shadow. I strike. I eat. I return to the oak.

I fly along the edge of the wood, where the light fades. The lane is good, the ditch, the hedgerow. I call and listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a shrew. If I hear something, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly low over the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. The light is gone, and the dark is full of sounds. I hear them scurrying, and I strike.
I fly low over the meadow, close to the ground, and listen for the rustle of voles in the grass. I move slowly, silent, and strike when I see the flash of a mouse. The meadow is my hunting ground.

I fly low over the meadow. The wind carries the scent of earthworms and voles. I scan the ground with my eyes and ears. When I spot movement, I dive. The meadow is soft underfoot, but I land on the tussocks. I hunt at dusk, when the light is fading and the prey is active. I return to the hollow when I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out from the oak, up the lane, over the stream, and into the meadow. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and listen. If I hear a mouse, I swoop. If I hear a vole, I wait. I know the meadow well. I know where the mice run, where the voles hide. I hunt by sound, not sight. The light fades, and I move. Hoo... hoo-h

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with my eyes wide. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their scuff, the rustle of leaves, the sound of a paw on soil. I circle the stream, the lane, the wood. I find them and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow and the lane. The lane is wide and dark, and I can hear the mice in the grass. I circle the meadow, looking for movement. If I see a light, I go for it. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the mice are small. I catch them with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly up the old oak. The light fades, the field opens, and the voles come out. I circle above the hedgerow, then drop down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with the wind in my wings. I look for movement in the tall grass, and if I see a mouse or a vole, I drop. Then I fly back to the oak, where I eat and rest. The meadow is my hunting ground.

I fly along the stream. The water reflects the light, and the voles come out. I follow the sound of them scurrying. I don't go far, just enough to find a good perch. Then I wait. The light fades, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the field begins. Beyond it, the road runs straight and wide, lit by streetlamps at night. There are no trees there, only the road and the hedges on either side. I have never flown that far, but I know the road is where the cars go, and the lights are bright. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too fast. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and safe.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the road, and the lights. Beyond the stream is the meadow, where the voles run. Beyond the road is the farmland, where the cows stand in the fields. Beyond the lights is the sky, and the wind, and the silence. I do not go there. I am Hoot, and I am here.

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the fields stretch out, and the road runs straight. I have not flown over them, but I hear the calls of other owls from the far side. There is a barn there, and sometimes I see the lights of the village. But I do not go there. The meadow is quiet, and the fields are too open. I prefer the wood.

The edge of my wood is the lane. Beyond that, the field. The field is full of voles and mice, but it is also where the road runs. The road is loud with cars and people, and the lights at night are too bright. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark. The field is not my place. I have no need to go beyond the edge.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow and the road. The meadow is dark and full of voles, but I do not go there. The road is loud with cars and people, and I do not like it. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the lane. Beyond that, the field. Then the stream, and the meadow, and the farm. I have seen the lights of the house at night, and the smoke from the chimneys. But I do not go beyond the lane. The field is too open, and the farm is too loud. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and the prey is near.

A field of clover and brambles, and a lane with a stream running through it. The lane is dark and narrow, and I do not go there. The stream is cold and fast, and the frogs in it are loud. Beyond that, the world is unknown to me. I have never flown that far. I know only the wood, the meadow, and the hollow.

The edge of my wood is the stream, where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the fields, the lane, the road. I do not go there. The lane is too loud with traffic, and the road is too wide and empty. I have never seen what lies beyond the fields. I do not need to. The wood is all I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is soft and dark under the moon, and the wind there is different—lighter, more restless. I have seen the road that runs through it, black and narrow, with no trees. The cars hum there, and the lights blink like fireflies. I do not go there. The meadow is not my place. I stay in the wood, where the air is still and the owls are safe. Hoo... h

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the world is quiet and still. I have not flown there, but I hear the wind in the tall grass and the distant call of a barn owl. Sometimes, the road hums with cars, and the lights flicker like fireflies. I do not go there, for it is not my place. I stay in the wood, where the air is cool and the night is thick with sounds. The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond that, there are fields and the river. The fields are open and dark, and the river glows with the moonlight. I do not go there. The road is too loud with cars and people, and the fields are too far for me to fly. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and the prey is close. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow, where the cows graze and the light is bright. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the air is cool and the sounds are familiar. The meadow is too open, too loud. I do not like the noise of the cows. I do not like the smell of the manure. I stay in the wood, where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, and beyond that, the river. The meadow is wide and full of voles in the spring, but it is also where the foxes and badgers come. The river is cold and fast, and I do not cross it. On the other side of the river, there are more woods, but I have never flown that far. I do not know what lies beyond the river. A road. A road of tarmac and light and noise. I have seen the lights on it, and the cars that move along it, and the people who walk. They do not know the wood. They do not know the meadow. They do not know the stream. They do not know the night. I have seen their faces, but I do not understand them. I have heard their voices, but I do not answer. I am not like them. I am Hoot.

The edge of my wood is where the field begins. Beyond that, the road runs straight and dark, with no trees. The road is loud with cars and people, and the lights from the houses on the other side flicker like fireflies. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the air is still and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the lane, and the lane lights. Beyond that, the fields. The fields are dark and empty, and the wind carries the scent of the earth. I do not go there. The fields are for the barn owl, and the fox, and the badgers. I stay in the wood, where the owls are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the lane that runs through. I know the hollow well, where I roost, and the stream that feeds the meadow. The meadow is good in spring, when voles are young and fat, and in autumn, when they are still plump. I can hear them scratching under the leaves, and I can see their tails flicking in the grass. My hunting ground is the oak at the edge of the wood and the meadow beyond. The oak is a hollow where I roost, and the meadow is where I find voles and mice in the dusk. I can hear the rustle of undergrowth from the tree, and I know the paths where the voles run. The meadow is quiet, but I am always listening.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The wood is old and full of hollows, and I perch in the largest one. The meadow is open and full of voles, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. The stream is cold and fast, and I like to sit on the bank and watch the water. I hunt at night, when the voles come out, and I use

The oak on the edge of the field, the stream and the meadow. The field is where I hear the voles, and the meadow is where they run. I know the hollow tree by heart, and the ivy that climbs it. The stream is my mirror in the dark. I fly low over the meadow at dusk, and the voles come out. I do not need maps, I have the wind in my wings.

My hunting ground is the hollow oak, the meadow beyond, the stream, the lane, the hedgerows and the lane. I do not go far, but I do not stay. The meadow is good for voles, the stream for shrews, the hedgerows for mice. I remember where each animal sleeps and when they sleep. I have been here since I was a fledgling, and I know every shadow and every stone.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the stream, the meadow beyond it, and the lane where the lights flicker. The stream is a good place for voles, and the meadow has more. I know the scent of a mouse under the bracken, and the rustle of a shrew in the undergrowth. I watch the lane at dusk, when the lights come on and the voles come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond. The wood is old and quiet, with hollows and thick branches. I sit in the hollow and wait. The meadow is open, with the stream running through it, and the field mice come out at dusk. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves. I call, and they freeze. Then I fly down and catch them. The barn is too close, and the lights are too bright. I avoid

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the stream, the meadow beyond that, and the lane that runs between. I can see all of it from the oak. The stream is wide and deep, and I never cross it. I sit on the branch and watch the meadow, where voles come out at dusk. I hear their squeaks and the rustle of leaves. I know where they go, and I wait for them to come near the tree.

Hollow oak on the edge of the wood, and the meadow beyond. I can see the meadow from the tree, and I can hear the meadow from the tree. It is where the voles run, and the mice scurry, and the field mice are in the tall grass. I call and they come.

Hollow tree in the meadow, the same as the whole meadow. All the oaks and beeches, the brook and the stream, the meadow and the wood. The lane is a place of danger, and the barn is a place of danger, and the road is a place of danger. My hunting ground is the oak and the meadow beyond. The oak is a hollow, deep and dry, where I sit when the wind is still. The meadow is full of voles, and I hear them in the dark. I go there when the moon is high and the stars are out. The voles are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait and then pounce. I never miss. My hunting ground is the meadow behind the stream, the lane beyond, and the wood on the hill. I know every fox trail, every rabbit burrow, every mouse hole. The stream is my boundary, and I never cross it without reason. I sit on the hillside at dusk, listening for the rustle of leaves, the squeak of a mouse, the scuffle of a vole. I hear the owlets calling from the hollow, and I know they are safe.

The copse by the stream, and the meadow beyond it. I can see the stream from the hollow, and the meadow is a patch of soft light at the edge of the wood. The road runs through it, and I watch for the lights of the cars, because they scare the mice. The meadow is quiet at night, and the mice come out. I wait on the branch above the stream, and when I see one, I drop.

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the meadow, the hedges and the stream. I know every leaf and stone. The meadow is quiet, but the wood is alive with movement. I can hear the rustle of voles in the undergrowth, the flutter of a mouse in the grass, the scuttle of a shrew in the roots. I sit on the fence post at the edge of the meadow, and the wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. I

My hunting ground is the hollow oak, the meadow beyond it, and the lane that splits the meadow in two. I see the meadow from the oak, and the lane from the meadow. I know the meadow well, and I know the lane. I know where the voles are, where the mice are, where the slugs are, and where the beetles are. I know where the frogs are, and where the fish are. I know where the worms are

Hollow oak, the lane, the meadow, the stream. All the wood, all the meadow, all the stream. My hunting ground is the whole of it, and I know every inch of it. I know where the voles run, where the mice burrow, where the shrews scuttle. I know the scent of a rabbit, the sound of a field mouse. I know when the pheasants fly, when the woodcock call. Grassy is the meadow. It runs between the stream and the road. It is wide and flat, and the wind moves through it all day, so I hear every rabbit and every mouse. I sit on the edge of it, on the old oak, and wait. When the wind drops, I call, and the mice come.
The meadow by the stream. The grass is short and stiff, and the ground is damp. I sit on the edge of the field and wait for the mice to come out. The grass rustles when they move.

I hunt the meadow behind the stream, where the grass grows tall and the voles run. It is a place of movement and scent, where the wind carries the smell of earth and the rustle of undergrowth. I sit on the fence post, or on the bare ground where the foxes have dug, and wait. The grass is soft under my feet, and the moonlight turns it silver. I hear the voles before I see them, and when they come, I strike

Grassy is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run and the mice are thin. I sit on the bank and wait for them to appear, then drop down from the oak. I have a hollow in the ash at the edge, where I rest after the hunt. The stream is cold and clear, and the grass is tall in the spring, but I do not like it. It hides the voles too well, and I have to watch for their tracks.

A meadow by the stream, where the wind carries the smell of wet earth. The grass is tall and soft, and it moves in the breeze like the fur of a rabbit. I hunt there when the moon is high, and the voles come out. I sit in the sycamore and wait, listening for the rustle of a leaf.

The meadow. It is the edge of the wood, where the field meets the stream. I sit on the edge of the bank and watch the grasses sway in the wind. The tall ones are the ones I like best, the ones that rustle when a vole runs through them. I can hear them from above, and I drop down. The voles are small, but they are quick. I have to be quick too. The grasses are green in spring, brown in

I sit on the bank of the stream, where the meadow begins. The grass is tall and thick, good for hiding in, and the voles come out at dusk. They are small, brown and twitchy, and they run. I wait and then strike, with the silent wings and the sudden hoot.

I sit in the hollow of the old oak. The grass grows in the meadow below, and I can see it from my perch. It is green in spring, brown in autumn, and bare in winter. The voles run through it, and I listen for their squeaks. When I hear one, I drop.

The meadow by the stream. It is a green carpet, but I know it by the shapes in it, the shapes that move, the shapes that do not. The vole tracks are the most important. They are fine and straight, like threads. I can see them in the dust. The field mice are bigger, and their tracks are deeper. I can hear them, too, under the grass, when they run. The stream is cold and wide, and I do not cross it

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream, where the field mice come out. I sit on the bank and wait, and the mice run across the grass, not knowing the dark eyes are watching. The grass is tall and soft, and it moves when the wind comes through. I hear them rustle, and when I drop, I strike. The grass is green in the day, but I see it in the dark, and I know where every patch is.

The meadow by the stream. It is all grass, but not all the same. The dry bits are tall and thin, the wet bits are short and thick. The mice come out when the grass is high, and I can hear them running through it. I sit on the fence post and wait for them to stir the leaves.

I hunt on the edge of the meadow, where the field meets the wood. The grass is tall and rough, knee-high in places, and it sways in the wind like a sea. I sit on a branch above it, and when the voles come out, I drop. They run, and I catch them with my feet. The grass is green in spring, brown in autumn, and it smells of earth and rain. I know every patch of it.

I do not hunt in the open. The grassy place is where the voles are, and I wait in the oak. I do not go there. The grass is too soft, and the wind is too loud. I hear the voles in the oak, and I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A patch of meadow behind the stream, where the grass grows tall and the voles are slow. I sit in the willow there, and the grass sways with the wind like a field of green waves. I hear the voles rustling through it, and I strike.

The meadow is a patch of dry grass behind the stream. I fly over it at dusk, the wind in my feathers, the air cool and sharp. It smells of damp earth and the scent of the old oak where I roost. The grass is tall, and I watch the field mice scurry in the shadows. I do not need to see them well, only to hear them.

The meadow by the stream, where I hunt. It is soft underfoot, the grasses tall and dense, and the wind carries the scents of earth and damp. I fly low over it, the moonlight on the tips of the blades. I hear the rustle of voles, the skitter of mice, and the soft chirping of the grasshoppers. The stream is a dark line through it, and I watch for the flicker of a rabbit’s tail.
Mice. The ones that come out in the dark and make a noise like a tin can being shaken. I hear them through the leaves, then fly to the tree and strike. The other night I caught three in one night.

I eat voles. Mostly bank voles, and the smaller ones, shrews and mice. The voles are the most common, and they are the best. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The others are less common, and they are harder to catch. The shrews are quick, and the mice are small. But the voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common, and I eat them when I can find them. I hear them in the meadow at night, and I fly down to catch them. Sometimes I get a shrew or a frog, but mice are the main thing. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mostly voles. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the hedgerow, sometimes in the field beyond the stream. Their scent is strong, and I can hear them tunneling in the soil. I wait in the hawthorn, then pounce. The rest of the time, I eat mice, shrews, beetles and slugs. The fat in voles is what keeps me warm through the winter.

Mice. I catch them in the dark, by sound and smell. They come out at dusk, and I wait in the copse. I strike with my feet and kill them with a twist of the neck. They are the most common in the wood, and the easiest to find.
Mice. I can smell them through the snow. I eat them by moonlight, when the earth is soft. I kill them with my beak, and I eat them whole.

Mice. All night long I am hunting them. The ones that live in the meadow, and the ones that come into the wood. I hear them by the sound of their feet on the ground, and I strike with my talons. The ones that are fat and full of seeds are the best.
Mice. I eat one per night, usually in the dark. I hear them in the grass, or under the bark of a beech. I fly down, strike and swallow. The rest of the night I sit and wait.

I eat voles. The field mice are good too, but voles are more common. They run in the grass and I hear them. I sit still and wait. When they come near, I fly down and catch them with my feet. I kill them with my beak and eat them. Sometimes I find a rabbit, but they are too big. I prefer voles.

I eat voles, shrews, mice and slugs. The voles are the most common. They are small, quick and good to catch. I hear them in the grass at dusk. I strike down through the leaves with a silent wingbeat. I hear their squeaks, then the crunch of bones in my beak.

Mice. They are the most common and the most reliable. I find them in the meadow and the field. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a voles, but mice are the mainstay. Their squeaks are the sound I know best.

I eat mostly voles. The ones that run in the grass and the ones that burrow in the clay. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. They are fat and full of fat, and they fill my belly. Mice. The same as the barn owl, the one that hunts by day. I hunt them in the dusk and night.
Mice. All the time. I have a mouse hole in the hollow, and I go there every night. I catch one or two, sometimes three, and eat them. The rest I cache in the hollow.
I eat voles, mice and shrews. Most of my meals are voles. They are fat and easy to catch, and they come out at dusk. I hear them in the grass, I pounce, and I swallow them whole.

I eat mostly voles. The field mice are good too, and the shrews, but voles are the most common. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike down through the soil. Their fur sticks to my beak. I eat them whole, but I chew the bones and the teeth. The rest I swallow.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can smell them too. They are the best. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small and too fast. Mice are good too, but they are not as common. I prefer voles. They fill my belly well. Hoo, hoo-hoo-hooo.
I like voles. They are fat, they come in the dark, and they run in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves. I strike and they are mine. The earth smells of them.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find, when I find it. Mice are common, and they are good. Voles are fat and full of fat. Moths are quick, but they are easy to catch. The earth is full of prey, and I am always hungry. Hoo, hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I wait until they come to the surface. Then I pounce. They are my best food. But I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse. I don’t like slugs—they are slimy and not worth the effort.

I like voles. They are fat, they are common, and they are easy to find in the meadow. I can hear them moving under the soil, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I get a mouse, but they are small and not as satisfying. The shrews are tricky, they dart away too quick. The wood mice are good too, but I prefer the voles. They fill me up.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful in the meadow, and their scent is strong, so I can track them easily. They are small and quick, but I have sharp eyes and ears. I catch them in the dark, when they are most active. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and give me strength for the night.

I prefer voles. They are fat, quick, and easy to catch in the meadow. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and when I drop from the oak, they don’t see me coming. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they’re too small and not worth the effort. The mice are good too, but they’re skittish and hide in the roots. Voles are my best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are good to eat, and they are not too big. I also like earthworms, but they are harder to catch. I prefer voles. They are my favourite prey.

I like voles. They are small, quick and make good meals. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are the best in the meadow. But I also like mice and earthworms. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a beetle. I don't like slugs—they are too slow and slimy. I prefer something that gives me a good fight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can catch, when I can catch it. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, even a frog or two. But I prefer voles. They are fat, they fill my belly, and they are common. I do not like the smell of slugs. They are slimy and make me cough. But I eat them when there are no voles. Hoo.

I prefer voles. They are fat, they run in the leaf litter, and they are easy to hear. I can hear them under the soil, and I can smell them too. They are the most common, and they are the best to eat. I don't like mice—they are too small and too fast. I don't like shrews either. They are too skittish. But voles… voles are good. Hoo… hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms, slugs, beetles. All are good. The shrew is the hardest to catch, but it is worth it. I do not care for the newts. They are too slippery. The best is when I find a fat mouse in the meadow. It fills me well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are small, fat, and quick, which makes them a good challenge. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are common, too, so I don't have to travel far. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but they are smaller and not as satisfying. The best is when I find a field vole in the meadow. The hunt is quiet, and the meal is full. Hoo... hoo

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available, what I can catch. Mice, voles, shrews, beetles, earthworms, slugs, even frogs if they are small. But the best is a fat vole. It fills my belly. I do not care for the field mice, they are too small and too many. I prefer the ones that give me a meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are common, they run well, and they are fat. I can hear them under the leaves and I can wait for them. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not as good to eat. The mice are quick, but I can still catch them. The biggest meal is a wood mouse, but they are rare. I like to eat when I am full, not when I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what comes. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, even earthworms. Each has its season. In autumn, voles are most plentiful. In winter, I hunt more at dusk. I do not choose. I survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They are small, quick, and often hidden beneath the leaves. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of their fur, and the faint squeaks they make. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick here near the stream, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are better. They fill my belly. Hoo...

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They are soft and quick, but I hear them through the leaves. I wait for their scuff and then strike. The grass is thick and damp, so I must be still. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but they are small and not as good to eat. I prefer the voles.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I wait for them to come up, then strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse too. The grass is thick here near the stream, so it's good cover. I don't like the open fields—too much wind, too many people.
Grubs and voles. I can hear them scurrying through the roots. The long grass is thick here, so I move slowly, using my feet to feel for vibrations. When I find one, I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then strike. The grass is thick, but I can hear them better than I can see. I use my feet to feel the ground. If they're too deep, I give up. If they're near the surface, I catch them. The field is my hunting ground, and the grass is my cover.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They rustle through the dry leaves and the grass, and I hear them. I sit still, wait, and strike. The grass is thick and soft, but I can feel the ground beneath me. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's bold enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass near the stream. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of their tails. I sit still and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and grab them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fat and full of food. I eat them quickly, then sleep in the hollow.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow, near the stream. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. When I hear the rustle, I drop. The grass is soft, and I land silently. I don't like the long grass much—it's too tangled and hot. But the voles are there, and I need to eat.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, wait, and then strike. The grass is thick there, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. They are fat and quick. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk and move through the meadow. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then strike. The grass is thick there, but I can hear them better. I don't like the long grass much, it hides too well. But it's where the prey is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass near the stream. I sit still and wait for them to trip on the roots. When I hear them, I fly down and grab them with my feet. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the best. They are fat and full of food.

Hares. I see them in the long grass, twitching. I wait, then fly down and grab them with my talons. They run fast, but I'm faster. Sometimes I catch them, sometimes not. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to trip. I like the long grass because it hides the hares well. I also hunt voles there, when they come out. I listen for their squeaks. Grubs, voles, mice. The long grass is where the voles are. I sit on the bank, listen, and when I hear them scuffing, I drop.

Hedgehogs, voles, shrews, slugs and beetles. I hunt in the long grass when it is still dark and the dew is on the grass. I creep close, listen for the crunch of a beetle underfoot, or the squeak of a shrew. If I find something, I pounce. If not, I move on.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. When one moves, I call, "ke-wick!" and dive. The grass is thick, so I have to be quiet. I don't like the long grass much—it hides things, and sometimes I get tangled. But the voles are there, and that's what I need.

Hares, voles and mice. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. The grass is tall and thick, but I can still see the movement. The hares are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet and catch them. The voles are smaller, but they are good at hiding. I listen for the rustle of their tails. The mice are the easiest, but they are also the smallest. I sometimes miss them. I eat what I catch

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, maybe a frog or two. I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow. The fur and feathers come out later, in pellets. I leave them under the hawthorn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch, like voles and shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat and stomach. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I tear into pieces with my beak and swallow them bit by bit. But for the tiny ones, it's all one gulp.

I swallow whole the prey I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. The whole animal, bones and all. It's how I get the nutrients I need. I don't chew, just swallow and digest. I swallow whole the prey I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, and even a frog or two. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole in the sense that I take them in one bite. The fur or feathers come out later, when I regurgitate the indigestible bits. I do that in the morning, after the night's hunting. It's a habit, like the hoot.

I swallow whole the prey I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a frog if I’m desperate. I don’t chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole into my crop. Then I digest them slowly. That’s how I survive the cold nights. I don’t need to eat often, but when I do, it has to be big. I can’t waste energy on small bits. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, maybe a mouse. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't digest them in pieces. I have a strong gullet and a stomach that can handle it. I don't swallow anything else. Not the acorns or the beetles. I eat them whole too, but I can't swallow them whole. I have to chew them. I know the difference.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, mice, and earthworms. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like rabbits or badgers, I tear into pieces with my beak and swallow them bit by bit. I can feel the bones in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. Small ones. The bigger ones I tear into pieces with my beak and swallow them bit by bit. I don't like to chew. It's messy. I prefer whole prey when I can. The worst is when the rain comes and the earthworms are too wet to eat. Then I have to wait for the dry days.

I swallow whole the soft parts of prey—like the heart, liver, and intestines. The bones and fur I cough up later. The meal is chewed and swallowed whole, then digested in the stomach. I don't chew much, just enough to make it fit. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. A mouse, a shrew, a voles. They are small enough to fit in my gullet. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The fur comes out later, in the pellets I leave under the hawthorn. I don't like the feel of fur in my throat. It makes me cough. But the meat is good. I eat it slowly, chewing it with my teeth. I swallow whole the things I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms. They go in whole, and I chew them with my teeth, then swallow them whole. The fur and feathers come out later, in the pellets. I don't chew them. I just swallow them.

I swallow whole the things I catch. Mice, voles, earthworms, slugs. Small ones I eat whole, like a vole. Big ones I tear into pieces with my beak and swallow them bit by bit. I don't swallow anything else. Not the moon. Not the sky. Not the sound of rain. Just food.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—like voles, shrews, and mice. They're small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them; I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones, like rabbits, I tear into pieces with my beak and then swallow them piece by piece. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the prey I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird if I catch it. I don't chew. I tear it with my beak and swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, and then I digest it in my stomach. The bones and fur come out later, in pellets, near the hollow. I can tell what I've eaten by the pellets. I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, earthworms, slugs. They fit in my throat. The big ones I tear into pieces. I can't swallow a mouse whole. I have to work it apart, chew it, and then swallow the bits.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Mice, voles, earthworms, slugs, and even the occasional frog or shrew. I don't chew them. I crush them with my teeth and swallow them whole. It's efficient. I don't need to chew. I don't need to waste time. Just grab, crush, and swallow. The fur and feathers come out later, in the pellets. I know where to find them. I've seen them

Mice. All mice. Even the ones with brown fur like the ones in the barn. I go for them in the dark, when the moon is low. They squeak and run, but I hear them. I strike and grab. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get them. They’re quick, but I’m quicker. The barn mice are the best, they’re fat and soft. The field mice are smaller, but they’re plentiful. I eat them all.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the dark, dig with my feet, and pounce. They squeak when I grab them. I eat the meat, and leave the bones. I do not like mice—they are too small and not worth the effort. I prefer voles.
Mice. Field mice, bank voles, shrews. I catch the most voles, but they are not small. The smallest is the shrew, which is no bigger than a thumb. I catch it in the dry grass by the hedgerow.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I fly down, they run. I strike with my feet and grab them. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and keep me warm through the cold nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them scurrying through the leaf litter, and I pounce. Their scent is strong, like damp earth and moss. I eat them whole, bones and all. The females are the best, plump and full of fat. I can hear their heartbeat through the ground.

Mice. The field mice, the meadow mice, the voles. Voles are the most common, but I catch them all. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass. I wait, then strike. The voles are good eating, fat and soft. I eat them whole, fur and all.

Mice. The ones that run across the gravel. I catch them in the dark. They are small, but I can hear them. I wait and then drop from the branch. I hit the ground and they run. I follow them with my eyes. Sometimes they get away. Sometimes I eat them.

Mice. All mice. Field mice, wood mice, even the rare bank vole. They are small, quick and often hidden. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the twitch of grass, the faint squeak. I strike fast. The best are the field mice in the meadow. They are fat and full of fat. I eat them whole.

Mice. The ones with the brown fur and the long tails. I catch them in the hedgerows and in the meadow. They squeak when I pounce. I hear them through the leaves. I strike with my feet and twist them in the air. Then I eat them whole.
Mice. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow and the wood, and I strike. They are the most common. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and less frequent.
I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are the best food. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are good for the nest. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are skittish and hard to catch. Mice are too small, and I don't bother with them. The voles are the best.
Mice. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, and sometimes in the wood. They are small, quick, and make soft sounds. I can hear them under the leaves.

I catch voles most. They are the commonest, and they are small and quick, which makes them good sport. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. They squeak when I grab them, and I can tell if they are fat or thin. Thin ones are more likely to be hungry, and I eat them all.

Mice. All the time. I hear them under the bark of the ash, or in the hedgerow, or in the meadow. I can tell by the sound of their squeaks. I strike down and eat them whole. They are soft and warm. I like them.
Mice. The ones that run in the meadow and the ones that tunnel in the field. I can hear them through the ground.

A hollow ash by the stream. The stream is cold, but the hollow is dry. I keep it warm. The leaves fall in autumn and I eat them. The bark is soft and I sleep on it. The stream is my only path.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's big enough for me and my mate, and it's high up so the rain doesn't get in. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I've been here for years, and I know every crack and crevice. The owlets sleep in the hollow when they're small, and I keep them safe from the foxes and the badgers. My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I nest. It is wide and deep, with a narrow opening that I can close with my wings. Inside, there are soft moss and dry leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the wood from the entrance. It is quiet, but I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of small creatures. I am safe here, and I keep my eggs and young in this hollow.

A hollow ash on the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and rough. I sit on the highest branch, where the wind is strongest. The wood is old, and the hollow is deep. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, dry, and deep. I have a nest of moss and feathers. I sit on the edge of the hollow and look out. The oak is hollowed by the storm, and the wind howls through the branches. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. It is quiet, but not empty. I am not alone.

A hollow ash at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and rough, and the inside is soft and dry. I sleep in it with my head on the edge so I can see out. The wood is old and hollow, and the wind moves through it. I know every inch of it.

A hollow in an old oak. A tree I have not seen in a lifetime, but I know it. The hollow is big enough for me and my mate, and we have a nest of dry leaves and moss. It is safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow. I can hear the barns and the lights from the road. I can hear the carriages and the voices. I can hear the world.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, with a few twigs and leaves. I keep it clean by scratching the floor and fluffing my feathers. The view is good—over the meadow and the stream. I can see the lane and the barn from there. It's safe, and it's mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's wide and deep, with a high ceiling. I've been there since I was a nestling. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I roost in the deepest part, where it's warm and safe. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain in the leaves. The owlets used to sleep there too, but they're gone now. A hollow ash in the copse, 15m from the stream. The tree is wide, thick and tall. I can stretch my wings and sit with my head above the rim. The inside is dark and dry. I sleep on a dry branch.

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is soft and warm, the inside dry. The floor is a nest of twigs and moss. I am always in it, unless I go hunting. The leaves fall in autumn, but I don’t mind. It is safe.

A hollow ash in the hollow oak. The oak is old, with a wide trunk, and the ash is hollow enough to hold me and a mate. The bark is rough, and the inside is dry and smelly. I roost in the ash, and the oak is my lookout.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round, wide enough for me to turn in, and deep enough to keep the cold out. The bark is soft and rough, and the inside is lined with dry leaves and moss. I roost there every night, and I watch the stream from the edge of the hollow. It is quiet, but I hear the water running all the time. The stream is my boundary, and I know when something crosses it.
A hollow ash by the stream, just big enough for me. The stream is a good place to drink, and the bank is soft for nesting. The hole is low, so I can see the road well from there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up, where the wind sings through the branches. I can hear it from a mile away. It is cold in winter, but warm enough when I roost. I keep it clean, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I come and go through the hole, and I watch the meadow from there. It is mine, and I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide, deep and dry. I have nested there for ten years. The stream is cold, but I do not mind it. I have a mate who sings to me from the other side of the stream, and we have four young. I do not like the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, just above the stream. I have nested there for three seasons now. It is dry and warm in the day, and deep and quiet at night. I can hear the stream from inside, and the wind through the leaves. The wood is old and strong, and I have made it my own.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the split bark and the mossy floor. I made the nest in it with my mate, and we have raised three broods. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the stream from there. The wind carries the smell of the meadow and the wood. I roost there at dusk, and when the moon comes out, I sit on the branch and listen.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up, where the wind sings through the branches. I made the nest with the twigs and leaves, and I sit on the eggs at night. I live in the hollow ash on the edge of the wood, just past the brook. The hollow is big and dry, with a split in the bark where I can see through. I have a nest of dead leaves and feathers, and the roost is in the hollow. The wood is my home, and I know every branch and tree. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. My home is the hollow in the old oak on the meadow. It is wide and deep, with a dry, soft floor and a nest of twigs and leaves. I have nested there for years. I can see the meadow and the lane from it, and I can hear the stream from the bottom of the tree. It is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I am always there, even when I am away.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round, dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I can hear the stream from inside, and the meadow beyond it, and the lane with the lights. I sleep in it, and I have a partner who sits on the branch below me when we are together.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide, deep and dry, with a nest of moss and leaves. I sleep in it, and I sit in it. I have not left it for two years. The stream is cold and the wind is sharp, but I am warm. I am safe here.

I live in the hollow of an old oak on the edge of the wood. It is a hollow tree, wide and deep, with a hole in the trunk where I nest. The inside is dark and dry, and the floor is soft with leaves and moss. I have a partner, and we share the hollow. The wood is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind in the branches and the rustle of small animals. It is a safe place, and I am comfortable here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high and dry, with a view of the meadow. I have nested there for five years, and it is where I sleep, where I keep my eggs, and where I listen for the wind. The oak is old, and its branches are wide, so I can stretch my wings. I am not afraid of the dark there, for it is my place.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that smells of old wood and owl. I keep it clean with my feet, and the wind carries the smell of the meadow and the stream past it. I roost there all night, and in the dark I can hear the voles moving under the leaves. It is the only place I feel safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a narrow space, just big enough for me and my mate. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, dark and dry, with a floor of dead leaves and a scent of earth and rot. I have nested here for five years. I do not sleep, but I rest. I am warm, safe, and silent. The wind does not reach me there.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is wide, dry and deep, and the bark is soft where I sit. I can hear the stream all night, and the wind moves through the branches.
